newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria says to fight EU on anonymous accounts.
newsitem.headline: Austria says to fight EU on anonymous accounts.

text.p: Austrian Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger defended the nation's anonymous savings accounts against an EU call for their abolition and said he was willing to fight the case before the European Court of Justice.
"We have a legitimate legal position and so does Brussels. It will therefore be up to the courts to decide who is right," Edlinger told Austrian radio.

The European Commission will send a letter to the Austrian government on Wednesday setting out its position on anonymous savings accounts, an EU official said. The letter has been signed by EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti.
Unless the Commission receives a satisfactory response to its so called "reasoned opinion" within two months, it could take Vienna to the European Court of Justice.
Austrian media reported the EU was also unhappy that the government had avoided a total ban of anonymous securities accounts, preferring to phase them out gradually instead.
Critics of Austrian banking say anonymous savings and securities accounts are an open invitation to money laundering.

"Of course we share the European Union's desire to stamp out money laundering and that is precisely what our 'iceberg' approach does because it prevents people from opening new securities accounts," Edlinger said.

There are thought to be about 26 million anonymous savings accounts in Austria, a nation of seven million. The government and the central bank say the accounts, which have a 200-year tradition, are a key part of savings culture.
In August, when the government outlawed new securities accounts, existing accounts contained an estimated 400 billion schillings, of which 60 billion was owned by foreigners.
